subtitulo: The Greek civil war, the first battlefield of the Cold War, and the victors' state (1943–1949)

coda.heading: Coda for the trip: what to look for

items.text: In Athens, Syntagma Square, where on December 3, 1944, gunfire was opened on the demonstration: there is a discreet plaque. And the National Museum of Contemporary Art or the Benaki Museum usually hold material from the period. If you have time and stomach for it, the Kaisarianí neighborhood, a historic stronghold of the Athenian left, settled by refugees of 1923 and punished in 1944 and afterward: today it is an ordinary neighborhood with a very dense memory.

A conversational exercise, if trust arises, and carefully: ask about the EMFYLIOS, the civil war. It is still, eighty years on, a subject approached with caution, one where families still know which side each grandfather was on. Watch the register in which it is discussed: whether there are euphemisms, whether the subject changes, whether you are first asked where you're from. It is the same wariness one senses in Ayacucho when speaking of the eighties, and comparing the two will tell you a good deal about how a divided memory is socially managed.

In Corfu and Paxos, this period had less intensity than on the mainland: the civil war was chiefly a phenomenon of the mountains of the north and center. That relative unscathedness is itself a datum, and it helps explain why Ionian politics historically had a different profile from that of Epirus or Macedonia.

coda.next_hint: The next dispatch covers 1949 to 1974: the economic miracle and mass emigration to Germany, the system that physically built the Athens you are about to see, the parallel system of palace, army and embassy, the colonels' coup of 1967, the Polytechnic of 1973 and the Cyprus disaster of 1974 that brought the dictatorship down. And the most instructive contrast of the whole plan: in 1968 the Greek army staged a far-right coup and the Peruvian army staged a leftist one.

sections.heading: The civil war began before liberation
paragraphs: It is a mistake to treat the Greek civil war as a postwar consequence. It began inside the occupation, in the autumn of 1943, when ELAS — the guerrilla force of EAM, dominant on the ground — attacked the forces of the republican EDES in Epirus. The logic was the one that governs every plural armed resistance: whoever controls the territory at the moment of liberation controls the state that follows, and so the war against the occupier and the war over succession are fought simultaneously.

There is, moreover, an element that poisons everything that follows: the SECURITY BATTALIONS, Greek militias armed and paid by the Germans on the explicit argument of fighting communism, in which local notables, royalist officers and peasants threatened by ELAS requisitions enlisted. When the occupation ended, a good many of those men were never prosecuted: they were absorbed back into the police, the gendarmerie and the army of the new state, while the cadres of the resistance were persecuted.

That is the fact no conciliatory narrative can dodge, and it explains the ferocity that followed: in the Greece of 1945, COLLABORATING WITH THE OCCUPIER WAS LESS PUNISHABLE THAN HAVING RESISTED ON THE WRONG SIDE. Being a Communist weighed more heavily than being a collaborator. And here a warning against the reverse simplification is in order: ELAS too carried out executions, also imposed its power by force in the zones it controlled, also persecuted dissidents, and the strategic responsibility of the Communist leadership at the decisive moments was notably poor. There is no clean side; there is a very marked imbalance in who got to write the law afterward.

sections.heading: A piece of paper in Moscow
paragraphs: In October 1944, at a meeting in Moscow, Churchill jotted down on a piece of paper a proposal for dividing influence in the Balkans and passed it to Stalin, who marked his approval with a blue pencil. Romania, ninety percent Soviet. Greece, NINETY PERCENT BRITISH. Yugoslavia and Hungary, fifty-fifty. Churchill recounted the episode himself in his memoirs, with the remark that it might seem cynical to settle the fate of millions of people that way.

The percentages agreement explains two things. First, why the British landed in Greece in October 1944 and were prepared to fight the resistance that had liberated the country. Second, and more decisively, why Stalin gave no material support to the Greek Communists: he honored the agreement, counseled the KKE toward moderation, and when the civil war broke out openly, the aid came from Yugoslavia, Albania and Bulgaria, not from Moscow.

For a reader of international relations, this is the cleanest example available of how an internal conflict gets resolved by external variables. The Greek civil war was not decided by the internal balance of forces: it was decided by the British presence, the Truman Doctrine and the 1948 rupture between Tito and Stalin, which led Yugoslavia to close its border in 1949 and deprive the guerrilla of its rear base. The lesson for Peru is not that its own conflict was equally exogenous — it was not — but that the Cold War framework determined how it was interpreted, what support the state received, and which counterinsurgency practices were imported and deemed legitimate.

sections.heading: The Decembers, the White Terror and open war
paragraphs: On December 3, 1944, an EAM demonstration in Syntagma Square was fired on by police. Thirty-three days of fighting followed in Athens between ELAS and British troops — the DEKEMVRIANA — with thousands dead and entire neighborhoods destroyed. Churchill traveled to Athens at Christmas. ELAS was defeated in the capital.

The Varkiza agreement, in February 1945, provided for ELAS's disarmament in exchange for an amnesty for political offenses and a referendum and elections. The disarmament was only partially carried out; the amnesty, not at all. The period known as the WHITE TERROR, between 1945 and 1946, saw thousands of arrests, trials, killings by right-wing paramilitary bands and administrative purges against former resistance fighters. The March 1946 elections were boycotted by the left; the September plebiscite restored the monarchy. It was in that context that armed struggle resumed.

Open war lasted until August 1949. The Democratic Army of Greece came to mobilize tens of thousands of combatants, with a notable proportion of women among them. Its defeat had three converging causes: the closing of the Yugoslav border, massive American aid to the government — the Truman Doctrine was announced on March 12, 1947, with a package aimed precisely at Greece and Turkey, and was the founding act of the policy of containment — and the strategic error of the Communist leadership, which in 1948 abandoned mobile guerrilla warfare to fight conventional positional battles against an army supplied with artillery, aircraft and napalm by the United States.

The figures for the conflict as a whole are appalling for a country of seven and a half million: tens of thousands dead — the estimates vary widely, between eighty thousand and considerably more — around seven hundred thousand internally displaced, entire villages evacuated by the army to empty the territory of the guerrilla, and the evacuation or removal of between twenty-five and twenty-eight thousand children to countries of the socialist bloc, an episode the right called PAIDOMAZOMA — the same name as the Ottoman devshirme of dispatch 9, that is, the accusation of child abduction — and which the left presented as a rescue. Many of those children did not return until the 1980s, and some never did.

sections.heading: The victors' state
paragraphs: What was built after 1949 is the central subject of this dispatch. It was not a democracy with occasional exclusions: it was a regime that institutionalized the victory of one side.

The Communist Party remained illegal until 1974. The re-education camps of Makronisos and Gyaros remained in operation, through which tens of thousands of political prisoners passed, subjected to torture and to the demand that they sign declarations of repentance — the very same instrument designed by Maniadakis in 1936, as we saw in dispatch 20. And the CERTIFICATE OF SOCIAL CONVICTIONS became universal: a document issued by the police attesting to the bearer's and their family's national loyalty, required to obtain public employment, a professional license, a passport, or even a driver's license. It is estimated that the police kept files on millions of citizens in a country of eight million.

This means that for an entire generation, one's relationship with the state was mediated by an inherited political rating. Being the child of a former EAM member closed off careers. And it also means that the machinery described in dispatch 20 not only survived but was perfected under a formally democratic parliamentary regime, with elections, a press and limited alternation of power. It is the most forceful example I know of that the existence of elections does not by itself define the nature of a regime.

National resistance against the occupation was not officially recognized by the Greek state until 1982, when the PASOK government passed the corresponding law and put ELAS combatants on an equal footing with the rest. Thirty-eight years after the war's end. And the police files were not destroyed until 1989, through an explicit political agreement between right and left, in a public burning that was as symbolic as it was necessary.

sections.heading: Peruvian mirror: the postwar that was never legislated
paragraphs: The comparison with Peru is especially productive here because the trajectories diverge at the crucial point.

Both countries lived through an internal conflict with a Cold War ideological component, with massive state violence and equally brutal insurgent violence, with the forced displacement of hundreds of thousands of people, and with a geography of conflict concentrated in the poorest rural areas. Both produced a surveillance apparatus that outlived the conflict. And both developed a device of stigmatization that assigns permanent suspicion on the basis of affiliation or origin: the certificate of national convictions in Greece, terruqueo in Peru.

The divergence lies in how it was closed. Between 1974 and 1989 Greece carried out a sequence of deliberate political acts: it legalized the banned party, abolished the monarchy by referendum, put the dictators on trial, legally recognized the defeated resistance, and destroyed the files. There was no full justice, no complete truth — the civil war remained a difficult subject within families for decades — but there was a set of legislative decisions that removed from the legal order the status of internal enemy.

Peru had a Truth Commission with a rigorous report in 2003, and then it did not have the sequence. Reparations advanced only partially; convictions were few; the apparatus was not reformed; the device of stigmatization not only persisted but became more central to political debate over the last decade, and the norms passed between 2024 and 2026 on the statute of limitations for crimes against humanity and on the oversight of human-rights organizations point in the direction opposite to the one Greece took in the eighties. The Greek lesson is neither optimistic nor consoling: it says that closing a civil war requires explicit legislative acts, costly ones, taken against the very electoral base of whoever passes them, and that without them the war remains available as a political category for generations.
